units.title: Unit 53 — Cause and effect
learningObjectives: Distinguish underlying, principal and contributing causes from immediate outcomes.
Use formal and idiomatic combinations to describe causing reactions, disruption and change.
Explain direct, indirect, intended and harmful effects with precise collocations.
Describe convincing reasons, demanded explanations and serious consequences.

items.example: An independent panel was appointed to establish the cause of the bridge failure.
items.note: Establish the cause means determine what actually brought an event about, often after investigation.

items.example: Repeated outages stopped only after the engineers identified the root cause.
items.note: Root cause is the underlying origin of a problem, not merely a visible symptom.

items.example: The review identified excessive heat as the primary cause of the component failure.
items.note: Primary cause points to the main cause among several possible contributing explanations.

items.example: The new timetable did not have the desired effect on passenger waiting times.
items.note: Desired effect is the outcome someone intends; it does not guarantee the result occurred.

items.example: Residents may not feel the full effect of the tax changes until next year.
items.note: Feel the full effect highlights when the complete impact becomes apparent.

items.example: The delayed shipment had a knock-on effect on three other production lines.
items.note: A knock-on effect is an indirect consequence that spreads to other activities; it can be positive or negative.

items.example: The researchers found no evidence of long-term ill effects after the short exposure.
items.note: Ill effects are harmful consequences; here ill means bad, not sick.

items.example: The mentoring programme began to produce results after six months.
items.note: Produce results describes bringing about outcomes, often the intended measurable ones.

items.example: The proposal to close the public library is likely to provoke an outcry.
items.note: Provoke an outcry suggests strong and widespread public objections.

items.example: Unequal access to training can breed resentment across a team.
items.note: Breed resentment means gradually create bitter feelings, especially through perceived unfairness.

items.example: The inconsistent figures may plant doubts in investors’ minds.
items.note: Plant doubts suggests introducing uncertainty that can develop over time.

items.example: The sudden leadership change could prompt speculation about the company’s future.
items.note: Prompt speculation means trigger guesses or discussion without confirmed facts.

items.example: A cheaper manufacturing process could render the older machinery obsolete.
items.note: Render obsolete is relatively formal and means make something no longer needed or useful.

items.example: The signed agreement will set the wheels in motion for the new research centre.
items.note: The idiom means initiate a process involving several later steps.

items.example: Unexpected flooding could wreak havoc across the region’s farms.
items.note: Wreak havoc refers to causing severe damage or disruption, not just a minor inconvenience.

items.example: The alarm that beeps every thirty seconds is beginning to drive people crazy.
items.note: Drive someone crazy is informal for causing intense annoyance or frustration.

items.example: Another prolonged drought could spell disaster for small farms.
items.note: Spell disaster suggests that a situation is likely to have extremely damaging consequences.

items.example: There must be a compelling reason for cancelling the exhibition at such short notice.
items.note: Compelling reason is a persuasive or powerful justification, not merely any explanation.

items.example: Ignoring the evacuation warning could have dire consequences for nearby residents.
items.note: Dire consequences emphasises extremely serious, usually harmful outcomes.

items.example: Poor communication was a contributing factor in the missed deadline.
items.note: A contributing factor plays a part in causing an outcome without necessarily being the main cause.

items.example: The committee declined to give a reason for its unexpected decision.
items.note: Give a reason introduces an explanation or justification for an action.

items.example: The residents plan to demand an explanation for the abrupt water shutoff.
items.note: Demand an explanation implies a firm request, often when someone is accountable.

items.example: If the organisers ignore safety rules, they will have to face the consequences.
items.note: Face the consequences means accept or experience the results of one’s actions.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: The revised screening method may produce a positive result in the next trial.
items.note: Positive result focuses on a favourable outcome; a positive test result can have a different meaning in medicine.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: The sharp rise in cancelled appointments is cause for concern.
items.note: Cause for concern is a reason to worry; the phrase often appears without an article after be.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: The landlord cannot enter the property without good cause.
items.note: Without good cause means without sufficient or legitimate justification; frequent in formal contexts.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: The orchestra is giving a concert for a good cause this weekend.
items.note: A good cause refers to a worthy social or charitable purpose, not simply an explanation.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: The revised safety regulations will come into effect in January.
items.note: Come into effect is used when a rule, policy or change begins to apply.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: Sleep deprivation can have a detrimental effect on concentration.
items.note: Detrimental effect is a formal collocation for a harmful impact.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: She used a simple diagram to good effect during her presentation.
items.note: To good effect means effectively or successfully, often after a verb such as use.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: The pain relief may take effect within half an hour.
items.note: Take effect describes something beginning to work or have an impact, particularly medication or measures.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: The transport authority promised to investigate the cause of the signal failure.
items.note: Investigate the cause stresses the inquiry process; establish the cause stresses determining the answer.

items.section: D · Further useful cause and effect patterns
items.example: Some fish populations continue to suffer ill effects from polluted water.
items.note: Suffer ill effects means experience harmful consequences; ill here does not mean unwell.

units.title: Unit 54 — Describing groups and amounts
learningObjectives: Select animal collective nouns accurately for common groups of mammals, birds, insects and fish.
Describe brief feelings and complete ranges through collocations of degree and amount.
Choose idiomatic food portions and distinguish small from large amounts.
Use fixed expressions for collections, slight traces, strong streams and everyday measures.

items.example: A pack of wolves crossed the snowy valley just before sunrise.
items.note: Pack is the conventional collective noun for wolves and some other canids.

items.pt: uma matilha de cães de caça
items.example: A pack of hounds followed the scent through the woods.
items.note: Pack is also used for a group of hunting dogs known as hounds.

items.example: A herd of cattle was grazing beside the river at dawn.
items.note: Herd is usual for cattle and several kinds of large grazing mammals.

items.example: A herd of elephants gathered near the water hole at dusk.
items.note: Herd also works for elephants; not every animal group takes the same noun.

items.example: A swarm of bees settled on a low branch outside the greenhouse.
items.note: Swarm is typical for bees and other insects moving together.

items.example: A swarm of locusts threatened the newly planted crops.
items.note: Swarm is common for large groups of flying insects, including locusts.

items.example: A flock of birds circled above the station roof.
items.note: Flock is the standard group noun for many kinds of birds.

items.example: A flock of sheep moved slowly across the hillside.
items.note: Flock is also used for sheep, even though sheep are not birds.

items.example: A pride of lions rested in the shade during the hottest hours.
items.note: Pride is the established collective noun for a social group of lions.

items.example: A shoal of fish shimmered beneath the jetty.
items.note: Shoal is widely used, especially in British English, for fish gathered together.

items.example: A school of fish changed direction almost simultaneously.
items.note: School is another standard collective noun for fish; it often evokes coordinated swimming.

items.example: A pod of dolphins appeared beside the research vessel.
items.note: Pod is a conventional collective noun for dolphins and certain other marine mammals.

items.example: A pod of whales was sighted near the edge of the bay.
items.note: Pod is natural for whales travelling together, especially socially associated individuals.

items.example: A troop of monkeys passed through the canopy above us.
items.note: Troop is the conventional collective noun for monkeys and some primates.

items.example: A troop of baboons moved across the open grassland.
items.note: Troop is particularly natural for socially organised groups of baboons.

items.example: There was a flurry of activity in the newsroom after the results were announced.
items.note: Flurry suggests a short burst of intense activity rather than sustained work.

items.example: The unexplained departure caused a flurry of speculation online.
items.note: Flurry here describes a sudden cluster of rumours or guesses.

items.example: The exhibition attracted a flurry of interest when the reviews appeared.
items.note: Flurry of interest emphasises a rapid but potentially brief increase in attention.

items.example: We saw a flurry of snow before the sky cleared again.
items.note: A flurry can mean a brief, light spell of snowfall as well as a short burst of activity.

items.example: A flicker of emotion crossed the actor’s face during the interview.
items.note: Flicker suggests a momentary sign, rather than a strong sustained feeling.

items.example: There was a flicker of hope when the missing signal returned.
items.note: Flicker suggests hope appearing briefly and perhaps disappearing again.

items.example: The preliminary figures offered a glimmer of hope to the struggling community.
items.note: Glimmer suggests a faint but noticeable indication of something positive.

items.example: The explanation produced a glimmer of understanding in the audience.
items.note: Glimmer of understanding conveys the first small sign that someone grasps an idea.

items.example: There was a touch of sadness in her voice as she said goodbye.
items.note: A touch of indicates a small amount of an emotion or quality.

items.example: The speaker added a touch of humour to an otherwise serious discussion.
items.note: A touch of humour means a small amount of humour, often softening the tone.

items.example: The handmade invitations added a touch of class to the ceremony.
items.note: A touch of class is an idiomatic way to suggest added elegance or sophistication.

items.example: The documentary takes viewers through the whole gamut of emotions.
items.note: Gamut means the entire range; it commonly combines with emotions.

items.example: The fabric samples displayed a gamut of colours from slate grey to crimson.
items.note: Gamut can also denote a broad range of colours, tones or notes.

items.example: Reusing the old railway bridge was a stroke of genius.
items.note: A stroke of genius means a strikingly clever idea or action, rather than a quantity of genius.

items.example: Finding an empty seat on the last train was a stroke of luck.
items.note: A stroke of luck is a fortunate and often unexpected event.

items.word: not do a stroke of work
items.pt: não fazer absolutamente nada de trabalho
items.example: He will not do a stroke of work unless someone supervises him.
items.note: This informal British expression is normally negative and means do no work at all.

items.example: The café served the stew with a hunk of bread.
items.note: Hunk suggests a large, thick piece, not a thin neat slice.

items.example: The recipe calls for a head of garlic roasted until soft.
items.note: A head of garlic is the whole bulb containing individual cloves.

items.example: She crushed a clove of garlic into the dressing.
items.note: A clove is one segment of a garlic head, not the whole bulb.

items.example: The grilled mushrooms were served on a bed of rice.
items.note: A bed of food is a base layer on which another ingredient is placed.

items.example: Finish the mashed potatoes with a knob of butter.
items.note: Knob refers to a small lump of butter added to a dish.

items.pt: uma colherada generosa de creme de leite
items.example: The chef topped the fruit with a dollop of cream.
items.note: Dollop refers to a soft, relatively large spoonful of a thick substance.

items.example: The cook added a drop of brandy to the chocolate sauce.
items.note: A drop emphasises a very small amount of liquid.

items.pt: um pouquinho de creme de leite
items.example: He stirred a dash of cream into his coffee.
items.note: Dash suggests a small splash of liquid, less than a generous spoonful.

items.example: The warm pastries had a sprinkling of cinnamon on top.
items.note: Sprinkling is a small amount scattered over a surface, usually seasoning or garnish.

items.example: She put a thick slice of cheese inside the toasted sandwich.
items.note: Thick slice contrasts with a thin slice and denotes a broad cut of food.

items.example: The witness dismissed the allegation as a pack of lies.
items.note: Pack of lies is an emphatic idiom meaning many deliberate falsehoods.

items.example: There may be a grain of truth in the otherwise exaggerated story.
items.note: Grain of truth means a tiny element of truth, often within a misleading account.

items.example: That proposal does not show a grain of common sense.
items.note: Grain suggests even the smallest amount; this phrase is often used negatively.

items.example: The delegation reserved a suite of rooms on the top floor.
items.note: Suite of rooms refers to a connected set of rooms, often in a hotel or residence.

items.example: We bought a pack of cards for the long train journey.
items.note: Pack is standard British English for a set of playing cards; deck is also common.

items.example: The referee faced a torrent of abuse from angry spectators.
items.note: Torrent of abuse means a powerful stream of insults or verbal attacks.

items.example: Add a pinch of salt before tasting the soup again.
items.note: A pinch is the small amount of salt held between finger and thumb; the phrase also has a figurative sense.

items.example: After the run, she took a swig of lemonade from her bottle.
items.note: Swig is an informal word for a relatively large swallow taken directly from a drink.

items.example: He kept a pad of paper beside the phone for quick notes.
items.note: A pad has sheets attached along one edge for writing.

items.pt: um pacote de folhas de papel
items.example: The office ordered a pack of paper for the printer.
items.note: Pack of paper refers to loose sheets sold together, unlike an attached writing pad.
